messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi's eyes still widened in fear when he recalled the day his doctor told him he had stage IV cancer. It felt like it was happening right now, not two years ago. The numbness that initially enveloped him after the diagnosis slowly gave way to an overwhelming sense of dread every time the memory resurfaced. He would be sitting at his desk, reviewing policy briefs as a senior analyst, when suddenly he'd feel like he was back in that cold hospital room, hearing those devastating words. As Kofi struggled to shake off the memories, he became increasingly convinced that his body had turned against him. The constant tension in his muscles, the feeling of being on high alert even in his own home, all seemed to confirm this terrible suspicion. His body felt like a ticking time bomb, waiting to unleash another life-threatening crisis at any moment. He started to avoid certain tasks and situations that reminded him of his illness, like visiting friends who were also dealing with health issues or going for long walks alone. As he began to withdraw from social interactions, Kofi's feelings of isolation deepened. His wife had passed away a few years before his diagnosis, and without her support system, he felt lost and adrift. He became convinced that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again - the fear and anxiety had taken over, and he couldn't shake them off. Kofi's body seemed to be constantly on edge, as if waiting for another blow to strike. His mind racing with worst-case scenarios, he found himself repeatedly checking his vital signs, searching for any sign of trouble brewing. This hyper-vigilance only served to heighten his sense of threat, which in turn made the memories of his diagnosis even more unbearable. As Kofi's world shrunk, so did his ability to concentrate on his work. He was no longer able to focus on the intricate policy analyses that had once been his passion. The tension and anxiety had taken over, making it hard for him to sit still or quiet his mind long enough to complete even simple tasks. One day, while reviewing a particularly complex brief, Kofi's hand began shaking uncontrollably as he scribbled notes on the margin. He froze, staring at his trembling fingers in horror - was this another symptom of something going terribly wrong? The wave of fear washed over him, and for a moment, he was back in that hospital room again. It was then that Kofi realized he needed help to break free from this cycle of dread and anxiety. His fears about his body's reliability, the constant threat lurking around every corner - these thoughts had become an all-consuming force in his life. He scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping that she could help him rebuild some semblance of control over his emotions and his life. As he sat waiting for their first session to begin, Kofi's mind racing with worries about what might happen next, he couldn't shake the feeling that time was running out - for him, and for any chance at reclaiming a sense of peace.
